sm: This episode of Potomac Watch from the Wall Street Journal opinion pages covers the resignation of Nvidia founder and chief executive Jensen Huang after reports of an affair with a subordinate executive and a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Host Paul Gigot and colleagues Alicia Finley and Kate O'Dell agree the board had no real choice, citing legal and regulatory risk, congressional interest, and the company's earlier dismissals of the relationship. They discuss reports that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department officials about a Singapore-linked cloud firm suspected of diverting chips to China. Speaker Mike Johnson said Huang did the right thing for the company and the country.

The hosts turn to the espionage angle. Alice Huang has not been heard from since the story broke, and China's government has called the allegations a slur. Kate O'Dell and Alicia Finley say China runs extensive spying in the United States, and that Huang was a prime target given Nvidia's Blackwell chips, his access to the president, and his advocacy for cooperation with China. They call the case a wake-up call about Beijing building leverage through chief executives and rare mineral supply chains. They also raise questions about the Commerce Department under Howard Lutnick and about smuggling cases involving Super Micro and a Nvidia employee in Taiwan. Nvidia's stock fell 13 percent at one point, then recovered to down about 5 percent, after losing roughly a trillion dollars in value over recent weeks.

The panel says markets suggest Nvidia can survive without Huang, though he had about sixty direct reports and no succession plan. They compare it to Apple after Steve Jobs, and note President Trump suggested former Apple chief Tim Cook as a replacement. Competition from AMD, Google and Amazon may grow, and they predict possible antitrust scrutiny of Nvidia's circular investment deals. They see a chance for tighter export controls, with interest from both parties in Congress and bills already waiting in the Senate. They also warn that Democrats may use the case to push a tech oligarch narrative, amid public skepticism of artificial intelligence, including data center ballot measures that mostly passed restrictions.

The hosts discuss the argument that withholding chips will only speed up Chinese chip development. Alicia Finley replies that China is already spending tens of billions on its own chips, hampered by corruption and state direction, and that the real concern is Blackwell-class chips. They note a shortage of advanced chips for American needs. They then look ahead to a possible meeting between Trump and Xi Jinping next week, and criticize Trump's reported plan not to raise the Nvidia affair. The panel says the episode shows AI arms control with China will not work, and urges the administration to punish Chinese distillation and theft of AI models.
